title: The lost joy of monoculture
gist: Yglesias uses hard audience numbers — 2026 World Cup group-stage games averaging 5.1 million US viewers versus a 1990s sitcom flop that drew over 16 million households per episode — to argue that streaming improved content quality while destroying the shared-attention events that make consumption social. He connects post-monoculture atomization to franchise commercial failures, the rise of parasocial recap podcasts, and the political entrepreneurship of JD Vance and Chris Murphy, whose anti-growth prescriptions he rejects.

insights.claim: World Cup group-stage games in summer 2026 averaged 5.1 million American viewers each, while the 1990s NBC sitcom 'The Single Guy' averaged more than 16 million American households per episode in a first season that was considered a massive failure.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Quantifies the collapse in maximum achievable shared attention: today's biggest global sporting event draws a third of what a cancelled sitcom did, which caps the value of any 'mass reach' advertising pitch.
insights.quote: The World Cup group-stage games this year averaged 5.1 million American viewers each.
insights.locator: But even though the World Cup specifically is surely bigger

insights.claim: 'The Single Guy' was much more popular than any scripted show currently airing, yet left no cultural footprint or legacy at all — evidence that mass reach and cultural durability are separate variables.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Reach metrics alone are a poor proxy for franchise value; IP durability depends on something other than peak audience.
insights.quote: It’s just that pop culture used to be a routinely mass phenomenon, and even when it stank, it gave everyone something to talk about.
insights.locator: If you're a person of a specific age

insights.claim: Linear TV economics rested on schedule adjacency: viewers who watched both 'Friends' at 8 p.m. and 'Seinfeld' at 9 p.m. on NBC were very likely to watch whatever aired at 8:30, so the 8:30 slot was a launch platform rather than filler.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The structural asset streaming destroyed was involuntary lead-in traffic — the reason new-show launch economics are so much worse today.
insights.locator: Back in the linear television days, the schedule mattered

insights.claim: The tell for a failing show under the lead-in model was not absolute ratings but relative retention: 'The Single Guy' had millions fewer viewers than its neighbors and its ratings fell as the season progressed, so it was rapidly cancelled and the slot repurposed.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A cleaner cancellation metric than raw audience — retention versus adjacent inventory — which still applies to platform recommendation slots today.
insights.quote: Worst of all, its ratings fell as the season went on.
insights.locator: What you didn't want was The Single Guy

insights.claim: NBC cycled through failures in that slot including 'Caroline in the City' before landing on 'Suddenly Susan,' a show good enough to run four years but with no ongoing cultural presence — illustrating how much of network programming was disposable inventory.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Legacy TV libraries contain far less durable-value catalog than headline viewership history suggests.
insights.locator: NBC tried other things there that also failed

insights.claim: Streaming genuinely improved content quality and matching — Yglesias watched Kurosawa's 1963 'High and Low' and random YouTube fire-building videos from a Maine motel — so the monoculture argument is not a claim that entertainment got worse.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Separates the product-quality question (streaming won) from the social-utility question (streaming lost), which is where the residual value gap sits.
insights.quote: In most measurable respects, the entertainments on offer in this era were worse.
insights.locator: The convenience of streaming is undeniable

themes.theme: Communal consumption as the real product

insights.claim: The value of a mass event comes from parasocial co-participation, not the content: watching the same World Cup games with nobody on the couch, nobody tweeting, and no podcasters doing takes would be 'a million times less fun.'
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Implies live-event rights and second-screen/social layers are complements, not substitutes — the social layer is part of what viewers are paying for.
insights.quote: It would’ve been a million times less fun to live in a universe where I watched the exact same games but with nobody on the couch next to me, nobody tweeting about it
insights.locator: It would've been a million times less fun

insights.claim: The threshold condition for a communal cultural experience is not universal viewership but a large enough opt-in share of the population, as with March Madness or conversation-piece books like 'Yesteryear.'
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: There is a critical-mass threshold for cultural products where marginal audience converts into disproportionate engagement value — a nonlinearity worth modelling in media investments.
insights.quote: It’s not that everyone is watching the big game, but a large enough proportion of the population is that if you opt into it, you’re opting into a communal experience.
insights.locator: Halina wrote about this phenomenon with regard to March Madness

insights.claim: For conversation-piece works, the quality of the specific work can be almost incidental to the quality of the larger cultural experience it enables.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Quality is not the binding variable for cultural-moment products; distribution and simultaneity are.
insights.quote: the quality of the specific work can be almost incidental to the quality of the larger cultural experience
insights.locator: The same is true of conversation-piece books

insights.claim: Shared consumption functions as both a floor-raiser and a ceiling-raiser on experience quality: a bad 'Star Wars' movie seen with friends beats it seen alone, and good-not-great genre films like 'Tuner' and 'Crime 101' would have been better with post-movie drinks.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The social wrapper is an independent value driver — supports theatrical, event-ized and group-viewing formats over pure at-home convenience.
insights.quote: Participating in common activities is kind of a floor raiser in terms of how bad your evening can possibly be.
insights.locator: Those of us who didn't enjoy the movie on the merits

insights.claim: Post-monoculture, niche taste has negative social convertibility: at a youth swim meet in Waterville, Maine, the World Cup made good small talk with strangers while an old black-and-white Japanese film did not, whereas in 1997 network television would have served the same function.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Concrete illustration of why mass-reach live sport retains pricing power that prestige catalog content cannot: it is the only remaining common protocol.
insights.quote: And for that purpose, “Caroline in the City” is a lot better than an old black-and-white Japanese film
insights.locator: I was in Waterville for a youth swim meet

themes.theme: Franchise fatigue and a theatrical pivot

insights.claim: 'The Mandalorian and Grogu' had a shockingly poor commercial performance for a 'Star Wars' movie, and quality alone cannot explain it because Disney has released many bad 'Star Wars' films that performed better — something shifted in audience willingness to skip a release.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Franchise floor risk is rising: brand-driven attendance guarantees are weakening independent of film quality, a direct threat to IP-dependent studio models.
insights.quote: Something had just shifted in the culture in terms of people’s willingness to take a pass on a “Star Wars” release.
insights.locator: Earlier this year, The Mandalorian and Grogu

insights.claim: The combination of a strong overall box-office year with commercial disappointment for major franchise films points to a new era in which money is made by empowering younger filmmakers and telling different kinds of stories rather than churning out more superheroes.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A capital-allocation call for studios: original mid-budget slates over tentpole franchise extensions, with implications for exhibitor and production-company mix.
insights.quote: It feels like we’re entering an exciting new era in which there’s money to be made in empowering younger filmmakers and telling different kinds of stories rather than churning out more superheroes.
insights.locator: As a cinephile, I'm kind of glad

insights.claim: Franchise loyalty still monetizes through group attendance even when the film is bad: Yglesias saw 'The Mandalorian and Grogu' in theaters with his son plus two dad friends and their kids, and the outing was worthwhile despite disliking the movie.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Family/group ticketing is the residual demand floor for weak franchise entries — marketing to children still converts multiple seats per adult.
insights.locator: That being said, the marketing of the movie

insights.claim: The only show Yglesias follows episode-by-episode is 'House of the Dragon,' which he only somewhat likes, and his consumption is structured around Mallory Rubin and Joanna Robinson recap podcasts that are considerably longer than the episodes themselves.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Companion-content minutes can exceed primary-content minutes for a hit show — the commentary layer is a real and separately monetizable attention pool.
insights.quote: podcasts that are considerably longer than the episodes themselves
insights.locator: These days, the only television show I really follow

insights.claim: Recap podcasts now perform the function friends once did: where he watched 'Dawson's Creek' in high school to be in the loop for conversations with real friends, he now listens in on conversations between parasocial friends.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Explains the structural durability of podcast demand — it substitutes for a scarce social good, not just for radio.
insights.quote: Except instead of being in the loop for conversations with my actual friends, I’m listening in on conversations between my parasocial friends.
insights.locator: It's like in high school when I used to watch

insights.claim: As a podcaster himself Yglesias acknowledges benefiting from parasocial relationships in the other direction, and concedes podcasts genuinely fill the need for something to do while driving or unloading the dishwasher.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Names the demand substrate for audio — captive low-attention time slots — which is the addressable market ceiling for the format.
insights.locator: As a podcaster myself, I also benefit

insights.claim: Political entrepreneurs, in a theme running through recent books by both JD Vance and Chris Murphy, argue the building blocks of liberal politics and economic growth do not deliver everything human flourishing requires.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A cross-partisan intellectual convergence against growth-first policy — the ideological substrate for tariffs and sector-specific regulation from both parties.
insights.locator: I've noticed a lot of political entrepreneurs

insights.claim: Yglesias rejects the policy conclusion drawn from that critique, arguing authentic connection and strong community will not spring up as a result of tariffs or arbitrary regulatory burdens on private equity.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Flags tariffs and PE regulation as live bipartisan policy risks being justified on social rather than economic grounds — hardest kind to argue down on efficiency logic.
insights.quote: as if authentic connection and strong community will just spring up naturally as a result of tariffs or arbitrary regulatory burdens on private equity
insights.locator: Their takeaway, though, seems to be

insights.claim: The experiment of channeling personal disappointment, isolation and sadness into extreme political causes is now more than 10 years old and keeps failing to work.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Predicts continued political volatility rather than resolution — grievance-driven movements do not resolve the underlying dissatisfaction they mobilize.
insights.quote: It seems to me that we are more than 10 years into this experiment of channeling people’s personal feelings of disappointment and isolation and sadness into extreme political causes, and it keeps not working.
insights.locator: It seems to me that we are more than 10 years

insights.claim: The right framing is that progress generates new problems requiring new solutions rather than reversal: nobody in 1826 went to the gym because they did hard labor, and nobody dieted because they were avoiding malnutrition, so modern society had to build systems, habits and businesses around exercise and eating well.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Predicts commercial and institutional solutions to social atomization will emerge the way gyms and diet businesses did — a category thesis for community-as-a-product.
insights.quote: Nobody in 1826 went to the gym to work out; people did hard labor. They didn’t diet; they avoided malnutrition.
insights.locator: Nobody in 1826 went to the gym

insights.claim: The post-monoculture world is framed as yet another headwind to spending time out of the house talking to people, and the practical mitigation is to celebrate and participate in the mass events that still exist rather than trying to restore the old media order.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Supports demand for remaining large simultaneous events — global sport, tentpole releases — as scarce and appreciating social infrastructure.
insights.quote: We’re not going to put the toothpaste back in the tube, but we can probably do things to mitigate and compensate.
insights.locator: What I think we ought to do instead
